The bottom line of the present study – like
our previous 2015 judicial outcome study and
our three trial court studies – is that CEQA
continues to be a formidable obstacle to
building anything in California, especially
anything near where anyone lives. The cost of
filing a CEQA lawsuit continues to be nominal,
and the act of filing even a meritless lawsuit
results in multiyear project delays, which
either increase project costs or derail projects
altogether. Anyone can file a CEQA lawsuit,
even anonymously, for any reason, including
to leverage money settlements or other economic
terms. No costs or other consequences are incurred
for filing meritless CEQA appeals, even for repeat
offenders who file more than a dozen serial lawsuits
against the same project. The adverse equity,
consumer, environmental and public health costs
of CEQA lawsuits are generally not acknowledged
in court pleadings, although in recent years pro-
housing advocates have begun to file amicus briefs
in some CEQA lawsuits. Median home prices were
$197,8007 in Los Angeles County when a project
was initially approved in 1999; decades of litigation
later, homes are still being built, but median home
prices have skyrocketed to well over $900,000.8
Taxpayer-funded transportation improvements
are first stalled, then rendered unfinanceable as
project costs and delays rise steeply – and drivers
spend ever longer times away from their families
commuting to distant homes they can afford.

By Jennifer Hernandez, with Research Co-Authors Kristian Fors,

How an Environmental Protection Statute Has Been Weaponized
into a ‘Build Absolutely Nothing Anywhere Near Anything’
Development Blockade in California’s ‘BANANA’ Republic

Introduction
The California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) was enacted unanimously
by a bipartisan legislature and signed by then-Governor Ronald Reagan in
1970. CEQA is a catchall statute requiring state and local agencies to consider
environmental impacts before approving or undertaking a construction
project, plan or regulation applicable to a construction project or the physical
environment. CEQA is older than the Endangered Species Act, Clean Air and
Clean Water acts, California Coastal Act, National Historic Preservation Act,
and thousands of other federal and state laws and regulations that ostensibly
protect the environment and public health. Any person or entity that
disagrees with an agency’s decision to approve or undertake a project that
is subject to CEQA can file a lawsuit in state court. CEQA trial and appellate
court proceedings typically take about five years to complete, and while
litigation is pending, most approved projects are stalled.
Jennifer Hernandez has practiced environmental and land use law in California
for 40 years; teaches environmental justice, land use and environmental law in
California law schools; serves on the boards of several nonprofit environmental
and other organizations; and has published several books and scores of articles
on CEQA, land use housing, climate and other topics. While the author is grateful
for the research assistance provided by the Independent Institute and other
Holland & Knight attorneys, the opinions and recommendations in this study are
the author’s and should not be attributed to any other person or organization, to
Holland & Knight or any client of the firm, or to the Independent Institute.
CEQA increasingly has been criticized as a major
reason California can’t build enough housing,
water, and transportation infrastructure or public
service facilities – including important projects
approved and funded by taxpayers – because all
projects subject to CEQA must also comply with
myriad other laws to protect human health and the
environment, only projects approved by elected and
appointed officials can be challenged, and litigation
delays increase project costs and sometimes derail
projects altogether. In 2024, California's preeminent
government oversight agency, the Little Hoover
Commission, issued a landmark report describing
CEQA's past successes and present challenges –
and recommended significant reforms.1 In 2025, the
California Assembly Select Committee on Permitting
Report likewise acknowledged challenges posed by
CEQA in achieving the state's housing, infrastructure
and climate goals.2 The need to reform CEQA and its
national equivalent, the National Environmental Policy
Act (NEPA), was even acknowledged by Democratic
Party candidates in the 2024 national election.
CEQA reform debates are highly politicized
because powerful stakeholders exploit CEQA
lawsuits and lawsuit threats to leverage economic
or environmental settlements and judicial outcomes
that cannot otherwise be realized by laws and
regulations. Often missing from political debates is
how CEQA is applied in practice – including which
projects are being sued and how those lawsuits are
resolved. For the past decade, we have been filling
that gap with actual CEQA litigation information.
This report includes 11 years of previously
unreported data about the judicial outcomes of
CEQA appeals. It concludes with analysis of how
California Proposition 45 on the November 2026
ballot offers voters the opportunity to accomplish
what decades of legislative efforts have not –
meaningful, structural CEQA reform.

The most noteworthy conclusions from the
comprehensive data evaluated in this study include:
 The current study found far more CEQA appeals
filed and decided than were reported in the 2015
study. As reported by the Little Hoover Commission5
and informed by our own three trial court studies (as
described below), about 200 CEQA lawsuits are filed
annually. In 2015, which evaluated only published
appellate court cases as described below, an average
of just 14.6 decisions were issued every year. In the
current study, an average of just under 21 decisions
were published and slightly more than 24 cases were
not published – totaling approximately 45 decisions
per year, more than twice the rate reported 2015
study.6 Appellate proceedings typically take about
three years to resolve, and projects do not qualify
for construction or grant funding while an appeal is
pending. Filing more CEQA appeals gives project
opponents and those seeking to leverage CEQA
lawsuits for economic or other nonenvironmental
reasons a “free” and low-cost litigation pathway for
further delay or seeking to derail approved projects.
Appeals prolong the 18-36 months typically required
to resolve trial court CEQA lawsuits.
 Housing remains the top target of CEQA appeals in
both the 2015 and updated studies, as well as in all
three trial court studies, as confirmed by the Little
Hoover Commission. Infrastructure needed to serve
new housing or development – such as augmenting
water supplies (including through recycled water
technologies), wastewater and stormwater treatment
systems, adequate electricity (including primarily
renewable energy), and transit and transportation
systems – comprises most of the projects challenged
in CEQA lawsuits and appeals. These include climate
resiliency systems such as enhanced flood protection
or wildfire prevention projects.

LOS ANGELES
6 7
Background
 In the current study, far more “infill” projects
in incorporated cities or areas surrounded by
previously developed unincorporated county land
were challenged; 64% of challenged projects are
infill, about 8% have no locational flexibility (e.g.,
mining projects), and only about 11% of projects are
located on previously undeveloped county lands.
Besides resort projects, greenfield projects are
located at the edge of existing urban communities
or are served by existing backbone infrastructure
such as freeways and water supply systems.
 In the current study, agencies prevailed against
opponents at an average rate of 75% – still
rewarding project opponents with judicial wins
more frequently than NEPA and other administrative
laws. The most detailed, time-consuming and costly
form of CEQA compliance, environmental impact
reports – which can take two to three years – were
found deficient in 23% of the decisions in the current
study. “Addenda” to EIRs, which serve as updates
to previous EIRs, were upheld in 81.5% of those
decisions. As in the 2015 study, EIRs were far more
likely to be challenged than any other form of CEQA
document – about 53% of appellate court decisions
were challenges to the sufficiency of EIRs (including
a few challenges to supplemental EIRs). This EIR
challenge pattern is consistent with our 2015 study
and our three trial court studies.
 The current study showed more projects that
qualified for “statutory exemptions” under CEQA
statutes adopted by the legislature and for
“categorical exemptions” under CEQA guidelines. As
the legislature has expanded the number of statutory
exemptions for housing and homeless shelters,
an uptick in appellate court decisions challenging
those exempt projects has followed. Although both
datasets showed the appellate courts are more
likely to uphold exemptions, exemption challenges
comprise 25% of appellate court decisions, more than
double the number of exemption appeal challenges
reported in the 2015 study.

The bottom line of the present study – like
our previous 2015 judicial outcome study and
our three trial court studies – is that CEQA
continues to be a formidable obstacle to
building anything in California, especially
anything near where anyone lives. The cost of
filing a CEQA lawsuit continues to be nominal,
and the act of filing even a meritless lawsuit
results in multiyear project delays, which
either increase project costs or derail projects
altogether. Anyone can file a CEQA lawsuit,
even anonymously, for any reason, including
to leverage money settlements or other economic
terms. No costs or other consequences are incurred
for filing meritless CEQA appeals, even for repeat
offenders who file more than a dozen serial lawsuits
against the same project. The adverse equity,
consumer, environmental and public health costs
of CEQA lawsuits are generally not acknowledged
in court pleadings, although in recent years pro-
housing advocates have begun to file amicus briefs
in some CEQA lawsuits. Median home prices were
$197,8007 in Los Angeles County when a project
was initially approved in 1999; decades of litigation
later, homes are still being built, but median home
prices have skyrocketed to well over $900,000.8
Taxpayer-funded transportation improvements
are first stalled, then rendered unfinanceable as
project costs and delays rise steeply – and drivers
spend ever longer times away from their families
commuting to distant homes they can afford.

The debate over Prop. 45 is about California’s building future. Here is our endorsement | Opinion
By McClatchy Media’s California editorial board
Updated October 5, 2026 3:21 PM
Cows pasture on land near Scott Road and Carson Creek in Sacramento County on Wednesday, Nov. 27, 2024. Proposition 45 seeks to streamline CEQA for California projects like housing, water and clean energy, raising concerns about reduced review and potential environmental harm.
Hector Amezcua
hamezcua@sacbee.com
If approved by voters in November,Proposition 45 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/article317117913.html) would significantly change how California reviews and approves construction projects, including affordable housing, under the California Environmental Quality Act. CEQA, California’s most important land use law, has too often been weaponized by not-in-my-backyard interests (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/article316418885.html) to stop the construction of needed housing. (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/article316418885.html)
Prop. 45 seeks to bring long-needed reform to CEQA provisions that can add substantial costs to new homes, hospitals, water systems, roads, bridges and clean energy projects.
The initiative targets frivolous lawsuits and bureaucratic red tape that makes construction too slow and too costly. It proposes to streamline the permitting process without weakening the state’s environmental laws.
THE BEE’S VOTER GUIDE: Your guide to Proposition 45 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/article317117913.html)
Projects often make it through CEQA only to be stopped at the back end by litigation. Currently, a project can go through lengthy environmental reviews, be approved by a local government and still be sued under CEQA. In such cases, courts often order additional review, which adds to the cost of a project or, in some cases, spell the project’s end.
McClatchy’s California editorial board, representing The Sacramento Bee, (https://www.sacbee.com/) Modesto Bee, (https://www.modbee.com/)Merced Sun-Star (https://www.mercedsunstar.com/), Fresno Bee (https://www.fresnobee.com/) andSan Luis Obispo Tribune, (https://www.sanluisobispo.com/) recommends a “Yes” vote on Prop. 45.
“This isn’t about us running away from protecting the environment,” Dan Dunmoyer, president and CEO of the California Building Industry Association, told us. “This is about bringing what I call ‘the sweet spot,’ the balance, to protecting our environment.” Dunmoyer is right. Building more housing in California creates more opportunities for more people to stay and build lives with their families.
Prop. 45 would also limit parts of the CEQA process, including the often interminable length of public-comment periods for projects. It would limit judges from halting entire projects when they find a CEQA violation. Instead, judges would only be empowered to halt the portion of projects found in violation CEQA until corrections are made.
The initiative would also change the state’s tribal consultation requirements, limiting the mandatory consultation to only federally recognized tribes for projects using the new procedures, strengthening government-to-government consultation by ensuring early tribal engagement and enhancing confidentiality protections.
“Every year a project is delayed again means higher financing costs, construction inflation, legal expenses … and those costs don’t disappear,” said campaign consultant, Emma Manoukian Chung. “Prop. 45 (builds) more of what Californians need, and we stop wasting money on unnecessary delay.”
Those in support of Prop. 45 include the California Building Industry Association, California Business Roundtable, California Chamber of Commerce and California Council for Affordable Housing. (https://californiacouncil.org/) Those in opposition include the California Democratic Party, the State Building and Construction Trades Council of California (https://cabuildingtrades.org/) and Sierra Club of California.
By imposing stricter deadlines on government agencies to complete environmental reviews, Proposition 45 would allow housing, transportation, water and health care projects to move forward more quickly and at lower cost without weakening California’s environmental protections.
That’s the goal behind Prop. 45 — and it’s long overdue.

I'm weighing the Little Hoover Commission report as background: it's bipartisan, kept CEQA as strong protection, and called for "targeted and limited reforms." Its recommendation to limit data dumps and late hits lines up with Prop 45's cap on late comments, which is worth noting. I'm now looking at how the report treats deference to statute and CEQA guidelines.

I'm noting that the commission counseled against major changes at that point, and that CEQA litigation is rare, with about 200 suits a year against roughly two percent of projects, though a single suit can still hold up a project for a long time. I'm also checking how the Sacramento Bee editorial board came down on Prop 45, which seems to lean yes.

I'm checking how the Sacramento Bee editorial board came down on Prop 45, which seems to be a yes, and I want to see whether the LA Times board has taken a position too, since that would round out the picture.

I'm going to look at the Hernandez study next, since it seems to be the source for the cost figures on late comments and litigation defense. I also want to check where the $75,000 per-home savings estimate actually comes from, since the WSJ attributes it only to "estimates."

content.text: The Little Hoover Commission report is a bipartisan state body. It says litigation touches only about 2% of CEQA projects, and it cautioned against major changes before the 2024 reforms had been tested. Next I'll check the Holland & Knight study cited for the "$75,000" figure, and the Sacramento Bee's endorsement.

1
www.hklaw.com
Why California Can’t Build Reliable
and Affordable Essential Projects
California Environmental Quality Act
By Jennifer Hernandez, with Research Co-Authors Kristian Fors,
Scott Levin Gesundheit, Franklin Muñoz & Maria Daniela de la Rosa
How an Environmental Protection Statute Has Been Weaponized
into a ‘Build Absolutely Nothing Anywhere Near Anything’
Development Blockade in California’s ‘BANANA’ Republic
CEQA: Study, Sue, Rinse, Repeat
2 3
Introduction
The California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) was enacted unanimously
by a bipartisan legislature and signed by then-Governor Ronald Reagan in
1970. CEQA is a catchall statute requiring state and local agencies to consider
environmental impacts before approving or undertaking a construction
project, plan or regulation applicable to a construction project or the physical
environment. CEQA is older than the Endangered Species Act, Clean Air and
Clean Water acts, California Coastal Act, National Historic Preservation Act,
and thousands of other federal and state laws and regulations that ostensibly
protect the environment and public health. Any person or entity that
disagrees with an agency’s decision to approve or undertake a project that
is subject to CEQA can file a lawsuit in state court. CEQA trial and appellate
court proceedings typically take about five years to complete, and while
litigation is pending, most approved projects are stalled.
Jennifer Hernandez has practiced environmental and land use law in California
for 40 years; teaches environmental justice, land use and environmental law in
California law schools; serves on the boards of several nonprofit environmental
and other organizations; and has published several books and scores of articles
on CEQA, land use housing, climate and other topics. While the author is grateful
for the research assistance provided by the Independent Institute and other
Holland & Knight attorneys, the opinions and recommendations in this study are
the author’s and should not be attributed to any other person or organization, to
Holland & Knight or any client of the firm, or to the Independent Institute.
CEQA increasingly has been criticized as a major
reason California can’t build enough housing,
water, and transportation infrastructure or public
service facilities – including important projects
approved and funded by taxpayers – because all
projects subject to CEQA must also comply with
myriad other laws to protect human health and the
environment, only projects approved by elected and
appointed officials can be challenged, and litigation
delays increase project costs and sometimes derail
projects altogether. In 2024, California's preeminent
government oversight agency, the Little Hoover
Commission, issued a landmark report describing
CEQA's past successes and present challenges –
and recommended significant reforms.1 In 2025, the
California Assembly Select Committee on Permitting
Report likewise acknowledged challenges posed by
CEQA in achieving the state's housing, infrastructure
and climate goals.2 The need to reform CEQA and its
national equivalent, the National Environmental Policy
Act (NEPA), was even acknowledged by Democratic
Party candidates in the 2024 national election.
CEQA reform debates are highly politicized
because powerful stakeholders exploit CEQA
lawsuits and lawsuit threats to leverage economic
or environmental settlements and judicial outcomes
that cannot otherwise be realized by laws and
regulations. Often missing from political debates is
how CEQA is applied in practice – including which
projects are being sued and how those lawsuits are
resolved. For the past decade, we have been filling
that gap with actual CEQA litigation information.
This report includes 11 years of previously
unreported data about the judicial outcomes of
CEQA appeals. It concludes with analysis of how
California Proposition 45 on the November 2026
ballot offers voters the opportunity to accomplish
what decades of legislative efforts have not –
meaningful, structural CEQA reform.
2
1Little Hoover Commission, “CEQA: Targeted Reforms for California’s Core Environmental Law,” 2024, https://lhc.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/Report279.pdf.
2California State Assembly, “California Assembly Select Committee on Permitting Reform Final Report - March 2025,” 2025, https://a14.asmdc.org/sites/a14.
asmdc.org/files/2025-02/assemblyselectcommitteeonpermittingreform-finalreportwithoutappendices-march2025.pdf.
SANTA MONICA
4 5
Background
In 2015, I joined with my law firm
colleagues in writing the first
comprehensive report describing
CEQA appellate court decisions.3
We reported on all published
appellate court cases involving the
adequacy of environmental impact
reports (EIRs), negative declarations
and categorical exemptions decided
within our 15-year study period
(1997 to 2012).
3Holland & Knight, “CEQA Judicial Outcomes: Fifteen Years of
Reported California Appellate and Supreme Court Decisions,” 2015,
https://www.hklaw.com/en/insights/publications/2015/05/ceqa-
judicial-outcomes-fifteen-years-of-reported-c.
4The three comprehensive studies of all CEQA lawsuits filed in trial court over three distinct three-year periods include: Jennifer Hernandez, David
Friedman and Stephanie DeHerrera. “In the Name of the Environment,” Holland & Knight, July 15, 2015 (study period 2012-2015), https://issuu.com/
hollandknight/docs/ceqa_litigation_abuseissuu?e=16627326/14197714; Jennifer Hernandez, “California Environmental Quality Act Lawsuits and
California’s Housing Crisis,” Hastings Environmental Law Journal 24, no. 1 (2018): 21–71 (study period 2013-2015), https://repository.uclawsf.edu/
cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1032&context=hastings_environmental_law_journal; and Jennifer Hernandez, “In The Name of the Environment Part III:
CEQA, Housing, and the Rule of Law,” Chapman Law Review 26, no. 1 (2022): 57–158 (study period 2019-2021), https://www.chapmanlawreview.com/
wp-content/uploads/2023/05/clr_26-1-57-hernandez.pdf. These three studies are referred to herein as the “three trial court studies.”
5Little Hoover Commission, “CEQA: Targeted Reforms for California’s Core Environmental Law,” 5.
6Under California court rules, appellate courts have the option of designating a decision “published,” “unpublished,” or a mix of published and
unpublished sections. A “published” opinion (or published part of an opinion) may be cited as judicial authority in the briefs filed by lawyers in CEQA
trial and appellate court decisions. An “unpublished” decision (or unpublished part of a decision) cannot be cited as legal authority in legal briefs and
oral argument. In this study, we evaluate all appellate court decisions to better understand how CEQA litigation is used in practice and to identify
patterns in how appellate courts decide these cases. CEQA practitioners have long theorized that there are significant differences in the types of
opinions that are published versus unpublished (e.g., that agency losses are more likely to be published than agency wins), and this dataset confirmed
this theory. The dataset did not show any statistically noteworthy differences in outcomes or other criteria evaluated in this study.
Our 2015 report also described earlier CEQA judicial
outcome studies dating back to the first CEQA
decisions in the 1970s and contrasted the remarkably
high win rate for petitioners suing to overturn agency
project approvals with opponent loss rates in lawsuits
filed under NEPA, CEQA’s federal analog. We also
reported on a meta-analysis of lawsuits against a
broad range of federal and state administrative
agencies, which showed – as is the case with NEPA –
that agencies win nearly 80% of such lawsuits.
Finally, this current report was informed by three
separate trial court studies. Those studies tabulated
all CEQA lawsuits filed in superior court statewide
over three separate three-year periods (trial court
studies).4 Evaluating appellate court outcomes in
the context of all CEQA lawsuits filed in trial court
allowed us to identify practices that were not evident
in the 2015 study.
The most noteworthy conclusions from the
comprehensive data evaluated in this study include:
 The current study found far more CEQA appeals
filed and decided than were reported in the 2015
study. As reported by the Little Hoover Commission5
and informed by our own three trial court studies (as
described below), about 200 CEQA lawsuits are filed
annually. In 2015, which evaluated only published
appellate court cases as described below, an average
of just 14.6 decisions were issued every year. In the
current study, an average of just under 21 decisions
were published and slightly more than 24 cases were
not published – totaling approximately 45 decisions
per year, more than twice the rate reported 2015
study.6 Appellate proceedings typically take about
three years to resolve, and projects do not qualify
for construction or grant funding while an appeal is
pending. Filing more CEQA appeals gives project
opponents and those seeking to leverage CEQA
lawsuits for economic or other nonenvironmental
reasons a “free” and low-cost litigation pathway for
further delay or seeking to derail approved projects.
Appeals prolong the 18-36 months typically required
to resolve trial court CEQA lawsuits.
 Housing remains the top target of CEQA appeals in
both the 2015 and updated studies, as well as in all
three trial court studies, as confirmed by the Little
Hoover Commission. Infrastructure needed to serve
new housing or development – such as augmenting
water supplies (including through recycled water
technologies), wastewater and stormwater treatment
systems, adequate electricity (including primarily
renewable energy), and transit and transportation
systems – comprises most of the projects challenged
in CEQA lawsuits and appeals. These include climate
resiliency systems such as enhanced flood protection
or wildfire prevention projects.
4
LOS ANGELES
6 7
Background
 In the current study, far more “infill” projects
in incorporated cities or areas surrounded by
previously developed unincorporated county land
were challenged; 64% of challenged projects are
infill, about 8% have no locational flexibility (e.g.,
mining projects), and only about 11% of projects are
located on previously undeveloped county lands.
Besides resort projects, greenfield projects are
located at the edge of existing urban communities
or are served by existing backbone infrastructure
such as freeways and water supply systems.
 In the current study, agencies prevailed against
opponents at an average rate of 75% – still
rewarding project opponents with judicial wins
more frequently than NEPA and other administrative
laws. The most detailed, time-consuming and costly
form of CEQA compliance, environmental impact
reports – which can take two to three years – were
found deficient in 23% of the decisions in the current
study. “Addenda” to EIRs, which serve as updates
to previous EIRs, were upheld in 81.5% of those
decisions. As in the 2015 study, EIRs were far more
likely to be challenged than any other form of CEQA
document – about 53% of appellate court decisions
were challenges to the sufficiency of EIRs (including
a few challenges to supplemental EIRs). This EIR
challenge pattern is consistent with our 2015 study
and our three trial court studies.
 The current study showed more projects that
qualified for “statutory exemptions” under CEQA
statutes adopted by the legislature and for
“categorical exemptions” under CEQA guidelines. As
the legislature has expanded the number of statutory
exemptions for housing and homeless shelters,
an uptick in appellate court decisions challenging
those exempt projects has followed. Although both
datasets showed the appellate courts are more
likely to uphold exemptions, exemption challenges
comprise 25% of appellate court decisions, more than
double the number of exemption appeal challenges
reported in the 2015 study.
The data from our current study follows. Appendix
A includes a brief overview of CEQA itself, and
Appendix B provides additional methodological
information about this updated study dataset.
The bottom line of the present study – like
our previous 2015 judicial outcome study and
our three trial court studies – is that CEQA
continues to be a formidable obstacle to
building anything in California, especially
anything near where anyone lives. The cost of
filing a CEQA lawsuit continues to be nominal,
and the act of filing even a meritless lawsuit
results in multiyear project delays, which
either increase project costs or derail projects
altogether. Anyone can file a CEQA lawsuit,
even anonymously, for any reason, including
to leverage money settlements or other economic
terms. No costs or other consequences are incurred
for filing meritless CEQA appeals, even for repeat
offenders who file more than a dozen serial lawsuits
against the same project. The adverse equity,
consumer, environmental and public health costs
of CEQA lawsuits are generally not acknowledged
in court pleadings, although in recent years pro-
housing advocates have begun to file amicus briefs
in some CEQA lawsuits. Median home prices were
$197,8007 in Los Angeles County when a project
was initially approved in 1999; decades of litigation
later, homes are still being built, but median home
prices have skyrocketed to well over $900,000.8
Taxpayer-funded transportation improvements
are first stalled, then rendered unfinanceable as
project costs and delays rise steeply – and drivers
spend ever longer times away from their families
commuting to distant homes they can afford.
6
CEQA continues to be a
formidable obstacle to
building anything in California,
especially anything near
where anyone lives.
6 7
7"Median Home Sales Prices for Southern California, Existing Single-Family Homes by County, 1990-2025," Los Angeles Almanac, n.d.,
https://www.laalmanac.com/economy/ec37.php.
8"Housing Inventory: Median Listing Price in Los Angeles County, CA," Federal Reserve Economic Data, January 7, 2025, https://fred.stlouisfed.org/
series/MEDLISPRI6037.
8 9
Background
9U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, History of Smog Vehicle Emissions, 2024 https://www.epa.gov/greenvehicles/smog-vehicle-emissions#history
10“Active Transportation,” Southern California Association of Governments, n.d., https://scag.ca.gov/post/architecture-elements-active-transportation.
11See Hernandez, Friedman and DeHerrera, “In the Name of the Environment,” 22–28; Alastair Bland, “Weakling or bully? The battle over CEQA, the
state’s iconic environmental law,” Cal Matters, May 13, 2019, updated March 27, 2025, https://calmatters.org/economy/2019/05/weakling-or-bully-
ceqa-environmental-law-california-development-battles/.; Jason Barrett and Kevin Klowden, “The CEQA Labyrinth: Fixing the Flaws in a Good Law,”
Milken Institute, October 24, 2016, 4–8, https://milkeninstitute.org/content-hub/research-and-reports/reports/ceqa-labyrinth-fixing-flaws-good-law.
12Jennifer Hernandez, “Green Jim Crow: How California’s Climate Policies Undermine Civil Rights and Racial Equity,” The Breakthrough Institute,
August 16, 2021, https://thebreakthrough.org/journal/no-14-summer-2021/green-jim-crow.; Jennifer Hernandez and Lauren Teixeira, “Time to Reset
California’s Climate Leadership,” The Ecomodernist, January 6, 2025, https://www.breakthroughjournal.org/p/time-to-reset-californias-climate.
13California Budget & Policy Center, “New Census Data Show California Poverty Soared to Alarmingly High Levels in 2023,” https://www.
calbudgetcenter.org/news/new-census-data-show-california-poverty-soared-to-alarmingly-high-levels-in-2023/
14Public Policy Institute of California, “Homelessness Hits Record High in California, Jumps Dramatically in Rest of US” (2025) https://www.ppic.org/
blog/homelessness-hits-record-high-in-california-jumps-dramatically-in-rest-of-us/#:~:text=Californians%20have%20consistently%20cited%20
homelessness,24%25)%20were%20in%20California.
15Klein, Ezra and Thompson, Derek. Abundance. Simon & Schuster (2025)
8
Climate-resilient infrastructure to provide reliable,
affordable water and electricity are delayed for years
by CEQA studies spanning multiple years, only to be
challenged by project opponents intent on rejecting
approvals by elected officials – and then stalled an
additional five or more years in litigation.
Many stakeholders – the nonpartisan Little Hoover
Commission and Legislative Analyst’s Office
(responsible for overseeing state government
operations in California), Democratic and Republican
legislators, every governor holding office since 1990,
and hundreds of agencies and applicants seeking
to build anything anywhere – have recognized
CEQA as a massive obstacle or, as former Governor
Jerry Brown called it, a “blob.” CEQA’s status
quo defenders tout its necessity to “protect the
environment,” but thousands of environmental
protection laws and regulations are in effect today
that did not exist when CEQA was adopted in 1970 or
judicially expanded in 1972 to cover private projects
like building a home. The California Coastal Act, the
Endangered Species Act, the Clean Air and Clean
Water acts, the Occupational Safety and Health
Act, laws protecting public lands such as parks and
forests, and dozens of other major state and federal
environmental laws have cleaned up our air and water.
In 2016, the Obama Administration’s Environmental
Protection Agency announced that tailpipe emissions
of smog-forming pollutants had been reduced by
99%9 – without an electric vehicle mandate.
Today, CEQA’s staunchest defenders exploit CEQA
to block projects that comply with all existing
environmental protection laws and regulations. They
sue to get cash settlements to prevent new residents
from entering their neighborhoods or schools, to
oppose car-dependent development (despite the
fact that 97% of Californians drive daily10), to reject
market-rate housing in favor of exclusively taxpayer-
funded alternatives, to assert that unelected
community activists should control what can be
built anywhere, or to advance a vision of California
“de-growth” that prioritizes ideological climate
goals over actually reducing global greenhouse
gas emissions by making it affordable for people
and jobs to stay in California.11
Today, CEQA’s staunchest defenders exploit CEQA to
block projects that comply with all existing environmental
protection laws and regulations.
PLAYA VISTA
I have written extensively about the racially disparate
and regressive cost burdens imposed by California
climate policies.12 Defenders of CEQA’s status quo,
operating under the banner of the climate crisis,
have espoused ideological elitism while rejecting
any responsibility for structuring California’s climate
mandate measures “on the backs of working
Californians” – as California State Assembly Speaker
Robert Rivas reported in December 2024. In any true
“crisis,” we would build. In a state that purportedly
values equity and opportunity but has achieved
the nation’s highest poverty rate13 and homeless
population14 because we can’t build the housing,
infrastructure and public services we need, let
alone approve new manufacturing and other good-
paying jobs for those without advanced degrees
– we instead preserve a 1970 law that ceased
functioning as intended decades ago, shifting from
protecting the environment to obstructing efforts
to build affordable and reliable water and electricity
infrastructure and even benches at bus stops.
In a rule-of-law democracy, statutes are supposed
to be clear enough to allow everyone to understand
compliance requirements. If there is legal ambiguity,
the legislature or courts clarify. Here, with few
exceptions, CEQA appellate court decisions
continue to creatively and expansively interpret
CEQA to impose new and novel compliance
requirements on applicants and agencies to find

The debate over Prop. 45 is about California’s building future. Here is our endorsement | Opinion
By McClatchy Media’s California editorial board
Updated October 5, 2026 3:21 PM
Cows pasture on land near Scott Road and Carson Creek in Sacramento County on Wednesday, Nov. 27, 2024. Proposition 45 seeks to streamline CEQA for California projects like housing, water and clean energy, raising concerns about reduced review and potential environmental harm.
Hector Amezcua
hamezcua@sacbee.com
If approved by voters in November,Proposition 45 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/article317117913.html) would significantly change how California reviews and approves construction projects, including affordable housing, under the California Environmental Quality Act. CEQA, California’s most important land use law, has too often been weaponized by not-in-my-backyard interests (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/article316418885.html) to stop the construction of needed housing. (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/article316418885.html)
Prop. 45 seeks to bring long-needed reform to CEQA provisions that can add substantial costs to new homes, hospitals, water systems, roads, bridges and clean energy projects.
The initiative targets frivolous lawsuits and bureaucratic red tape that makes construction too slow and too costly. It proposes to streamline the permitting process without weakening the state’s environmental laws.
THE BEE’S VOTER GUIDE: Your guide to Proposition 45 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/article317117913.html)
Projects often make it through CEQA only to be stopped at the back end by litigation. Currently, a project can go through lengthy environmental reviews, be approved by a local government and still be sued under CEQA. In such cases, courts often order additional review, which adds to the cost of a project or, in some cases, spell the project’s end.
McClatchy’s California editorial board, representing The Sacramento Bee, (https://www.sacbee.com/) Modesto Bee, (https://www.modbee.com/)Merced Sun-Star (https://www.mercedsunstar.com/), Fresno Bee (https://www.fresnobee.com/) andSan Luis Obispo Tribune, (https://www.sanluisobispo.com/) recommends a “Yes” vote on Prop. 45.
“This isn’t about us running away from protecting the environment,” Dan Dunmoyer, president and CEO of the California Building Industry Association, told us. “This is about bringing what I call ‘the sweet spot,’ the balance, to protecting our environment.” Dunmoyer is right. Building more housing in California creates more opportunities for more people to stay and build lives with their families.
Prop. 45 would also limit parts of the CEQA process, including the often interminable length of public-comment periods for projects. It would limit judges from halting entire projects when they find a CEQA violation. Instead, judges would only be empowered to halt the portion of projects found in violation CEQA until corrections are made.
The initiative would also change the state’s tribal consultation requirements, limiting the mandatory consultation to only federally recognized tribes for projects using the new procedures, strengthening government-to-government consultation by ensuring early tribal engagement and enhancing confidentiality protections.
“Every year a project is delayed again means higher financing costs, construction inflation, legal expenses … and those costs don’t disappear,” said campaign consultant, Emma Manoukian Chung. “Prop. 45 (builds) more of what Californians need, and we stop wasting money on unnecessary delay.”
Those in support of Prop. 45 include the California Building Industry Association, California Business Roundtable, California Chamber of Commerce and California Council for Affordable Housing. (https://californiacouncil.org/) Those in opposition include the California Democratic Party, the State Building and Construction Trades Council of California (https://cabuildingtrades.org/) and Sierra Club of California.
By imposing stricter deadlines on government agencies to complete environmental reviews, Proposition 45 would allow housing, transportation, water and health care projects to move forward more quickly and at lower cost without weakening California’s environmental protections.
That’s the goal behind Prop. 45 — and it’s long overdue.

Placed on the November ballot by the California Chamber of Commerce, Proposition 45 seeks to amend the California Environmental Quality Act with new procedures for the environmental review of projects defined as essential.
The state law, enacted in 1970, requires public agencies to study and disclose the environmental impacts of projects before approval.
The proposition, if approved by voters, would allow project applicants to opt into a revised CEQA process that includes tighter, enforceable timelines for permitting and review periods, shorter windows for public input and changes to how courts consider legal challenges.
Specifically, public agencies would be required to certify final environmental impact reports within 365 business days.
Today, agencies have a one-year timeline to complete the reports, but the deadline is not strictly enforced.
The proposition would allow project applicants to compel agencies to finish the work and schedule a hearing on a project decision if there is a delay.
Proposition 45 also replaces minimum periods for public review with a maximum of 20 calendar days for comments on a mitigated or negative declaration, and 45 calendar days for a draft environmental impact report.
And applicants would only need to identify a single project alternative to study, as opposed to a range of project alternatives.

I'm noting the Global ELR article from November 2, 2026. Its key point is that the measure would take effect on the fifth day after the Secretary of State files the statement of the vote, and that it would reach not only new applications but also agency proceedings and lawsuits already underway. I'm also looking at its voluntary structure: applicants could choose none, some, or all of the provisions, subject to mandatory tribal consultation.

I'm working through whether the opt-in reading matters for the decision. Since the judicial limits are a major benefit, developers would likely choose to adopt the full package, which means the big changes would reach most essential projects where a developer is involved.

I'm checking the data center question next: the No side says developers gave about $1M to Yes in the final week, and the Legislative Counsel letter is disputed, since Yes cites it while No says it never addressed Prop 45 specifically. I'm treating that as unresolved and likely to be litigated, and I'm noting a Verge article on the data center loophole. I'm also weighing the Daily Kos claim that the measure bars courts from stopping projects, which seems only partly accurate, because temporary injunctions remain possible for narrow public-safety showings.

I'm checking the public-safety injunction language and the labor-workforce requirement in the statute, since the excerpt seems to bar prequalifying contractors unless they commit to a skilled workforce. I'm also noting the AP piece on the pro-housing split and the final PPIC poll, which had No ahead at 50 to 46.

I'm checking the labor standards next, since the housing exemption looks narrower than the general prevailing-wage rule. For essential housing, prevailing wages seem to apply only above 85 feet, so the labor concession is partly limited there. I want to confirm the wording of 21183.5(a) before relying on it.

I'm checking how the SB 35 prevailing wage rule in Government Code 65913.4(a)(8) fits here. The measure appears to narrow that requirement so it applies only to buildings over 85 feet in essential housing projects.

I'm noting that the measure's labor rules differ by project type: most non-housing essential projects would need prevailing wages and a skilled-and-trained workforce, while for housing the prevailing-wage requirement would apply only to buildings over 85 feet.

I'm going to check the labor code sections the measure references, since the statute seems to tie its labor requirements to 21183.5. Next I'll confirm the exact wording of 21183.5(a), since the prevailing-wage point depends on it. I'm also noting that the effective date follows the standard constitutional timing for initiatives, so that part looks settled.

Two useful details came out of this. The measure would apply to pending lawsuits and proceedings already underway, and the labor rules tie into Section 21183.5. I'll confirm exactly what 21183.5 requires, since the labor provisions matter to some voters.

DIVISION 13. ENVIRONMENTAL QUALITY [21000 - 21189.91]
( Division 13 added by Stats. 1970, Ch. 1433. )
CHAPTER 6.5. Jobs and Economic Improvement Through Environmental Leadership Act of 2021 [21178 - 21189.3]
( Chapter 6.5 added by Stats. 2021, Ch. 19, Sec. 1. )
21183.5.
(a) For purposes of this section, the following definitions apply:
(1) “Project labor agreement” has the same meaning as set forth in paragraph (1) of subdivision (b) of Section 2500 of the Public Contract Code.
(2) “Skilled and trained workforce” has the same meaning as set forth in Chapter 2.9 (commencing with Section 2600) of Part 1 of Division 2 of the Public Contract Code.
(b) (1) For a project undertaken by a public agency that is certified under this chapter, except as provided in paragraph (2), an entity shall not be prequalified
or shortlisted or awarded a contract by the public agency to perform any portion of the project unless the entity provides an enforceable commitment to the public agency that the entity and its contractors and subcontractors at every tier will use a skilled and trained workforce to perform all work on the project or contract that falls within an apprenticeable occupation in the building and construction trades.
(2) Paragraph (1) does not apply if any of the following requirements are met:
(A) The public agency has entered into a project labor agreement that will bind all contractors and subcontractors at every tier performing work on the project or contract to use a skilled and trained workforce, and the entity agrees to be bound by that project labor agreement.
(B) The project or contract is being performed under the extension or renewal of a project labor agreement that was entered into by the public agency before January 1, 2021.
(C) The entity has entered into a project labor agreement that will bind the entity and all of its contractors and subcontractors at every tier performing work on the project or contract to use a skilled and trained workforce.
(c) For a project undertaken by a private entity that is certified under this chapter, the applicant shall do both of the following:
(1) Certify to the lead agency that either of the following is true:
(A) The entirety
of the project is a public work for purposes of Chapter 1 (commencing with Section 1720) of Part 7 of Division 2 of the Labor Code.
(B) If the project is not in its entirety a public work, all construction workers employed in the execution of the project will be paid at least the general prevailing rate of per diem wages for the type of work and geographic area, as determined by the Director of Industrial Relations under Sections 1773 and 1773.9 of the Labor Code, except that apprentices registered in programs approved by the Chief of the Division of Apprenticeship Standards may be paid at least the applicable apprentice prevailing rate. If the project is subject to this subparagraph, then, for those portions of the project that are not a public work, all of the following shall apply:
(i) The applicant shall ensure that the prevailing wage requirement is included in all contracts for the performance of the work.
(ii) All contractors and subcontractors at every tier shall pay to all construction workers employed in the execution of the work on the project or contract at least the general prevailing rate of per diem wages, except that apprentices registered in programs approved by the Chief of the Division of Apprenticeship Standards may be paid at least the applicable apprentice prevailing rate.
(iii) (I) Except as provided in subclause (III), all contractors and subcontractors at every tier shall maintain and verify payroll records under Section 1776 of the Labor Code and make those records available for inspection and copying as
provided by that section.
(II) Except as provided in subclause (III), the obligation of all contractors and subcontractors at every tier to pay prevailing wages may be enforced by the Labor Commissioner through the issuance of a civil wage and penalty assessment under Section 1741 of the Labor Code, which may be reviewed under Section 1742 of the Labor Code, within 18 months after the completion of the project, by an underpaid worker through an administrative complaint or civil action, or by a joint labor-management committee through a civil action under Section 1771.2 of the Labor Code. If a civil wage and penalty assessment is issued, the contractor, subcontractor, and surety on a bond or bonds issued to secure the payment of wages covered by the assessment shall be liable for liquidated damages under Section 1742.1 of the Labor
Code.
(III) Subclauses (I) and (II) do not apply if all contractors and subcontractors at every tier performing work on the project or contract are subject to a project labor agreement that requires the payment of prevailing wages to all construction workers employed in the execution of the project or contract and provides for enforcement of that obligation through an arbitration procedure.
(iv) Notwithstanding subdivision (c) of Section 1773.1 of the
Labor Code, the requirement that employer payments not reduce the obligation to pay the hourly straight time or overtime wages found to be prevailing shall not apply if otherwise provided in a bona fide collective bargaining agreement covering the worker. The requirement to pay at least the general prevailing rate of per diem wages does not preclude use of an alternative workweek schedule adopted under Section 511 or 514 of the Labor Code.
(2) Certify to the lead agency that a skilled and trained workforce will be used to perform all construction work on the project or contract. All of the following requirements shall apply to the project:
(A) The applicant shall require in all contracts for the performance of work that every contractor and subcontractor at every
tier will individually use a skilled and trained workforce to complete the project.
(B) Every contractor and subcontractor at every tier shall use a skilled and trained workforce to complete the project.
(C) (i) Except as provided in clause (ii), the applicant shall provide to the lead agency, on a monthly basis while the project or contract is being performed, a report demonstrating compliance with Chapter 2.9 (commencing with Section 2600) of Part 1 of Division 2 of the Public Contract Code. A monthly report provided to the lead agency under this clause shall be a public record under the California Public Records Act (Division 10 (commencing with Section 7920.000) of Title 1 of the Government Code) and shall be open to public inspection. An applicant that
fails to provide a monthly report demonstrating compliance with Chapter 2.9 (commencing with Section 2600) of Part 1 of Division 2 of the Public Contract Code shall be subject to a civil penalty of ten thousand dollars ($10,000) per month for each month for which the report has not been provided. Any contractor or subcontractor that fails to use a skilled and trained workforce shall be subject to a civil penalty of two hundred dollars ($200) per day for each worker employed in contravention of the skilled and trained workforce requirement. Penalties may be assessed by the Labor Commissioner within 18 months of completion of the project using the same procedures for issuance of civil wage and penalty assessments under Section 1741 of the Labor Code, and may be reviewed under the same procedures in Section 1742 of the Labor Code. Penalties shall be paid to the State Public Works Enforcement
Fund.
(ii) Clause (i) does not apply if all contractors and subcontractors at every tier performing work on the project are subject to a project labor agreement that requires compliance with the skilled and trained workforce requirement and provides for enforcement of that obligation through an arbitration procedure.
(Amended by Stats. 2022, Ch. 28, Sec. 137. (SB 1380) Effective January 1, 2023. Repealed as of January 1, 2034, pursuant to Section 21189.3.)

(iv) Notwithstanding subdivision (c) of Section 1773.1 of the
Labor Code, the requirement that employer payments not reduce the obligation to pay the hourly straight time or overtime wages found to be prevailing shall not apply if otherwise provided in a bona fide collective bargaining agreement covering the worker. The requirement to pay at least the general prevailing rate of per diem wages does not preclude use of an alternative workweek schedule adopted under Section 511 or 514 of the Labor Code.

(A) The applicant shall require in all contracts for the performance of work that every contractor and subcontractor at every
tier will individually use a skilled and trained workforce to complete the project.

Fund.

content.thinking:
I'm noting the Global ELR article from November 2, 2026. Its key point is that the measure would take effect on the fifth day after the Secretary of State files the statement of the vote, and that it would reach not only new applications but also agency proceedings and lawsuits already underway. I'm also looking at its voluntary structure: applicants could choose none, some, or all of the provisions, subject to mandatory tribal consultation.

I'm working through whether the opt-in reading matters for the decision. Since the judicial limits are a major benefit, developers would likely choose to adopt the full package, which means the big changes would reach most essential projects where a developer is involved.

I'm checking the data center question next: the No side says developers gave about $1M to Yes in the final week, and the Legislative Counsel letter is disputed, since Yes cites it while No says it never addressed Prop 45 specifically. I'm treating that as unresolved and likely to be litigated, and I'm noting a Verge article on the data center loophole. I'm also weighing the Daily Kos claim that the measure bars courts from stopping projects, which seems only partly accurate, because temporary injunctions remain possible for narrow public-safety showings.

I'm checking the public-safety injunction language and the labor-workforce requirement in the statute, since the excerpt seems to bar prequalifying contractors unless they commit to a skilled workforce. I'm also noting the AP piece on the pro-housing split and the final PPIC poll, which had No ahead at 50 to 46.

I'm checking the labor standards next, since the housing exemption looks narrower than the general prevailing-wage rule. For essential housing, prevailing wages seem to apply only above 85 feet, so the labor concession is partly limited there. I want to confirm the wording of 21183.5(a) before relying on it.

I'm checking how the SB 35 prevailing wage rule in Government Code 65913.4(a)(8) fits here. The measure appears to narrow that requirement so it applies only to buildings over 85 feet in essential housing projects.

I'm noting that the measure's labor rules differ by project type: most non-housing essential projects would need prevailing wages and a skilled-and-trained workforce, while for housing the prevailing-wage requirement would apply only to buildings over 85 feet.

I'm going to check the labor code sections the measure references, since the statute seems to tie its labor requirements to 21183.5. Next I'll confirm the exact wording of 21183.5(a), since the prevailing-wage point depends on it. I'm also noting that the effective date follows the standard constitutional timing for initiatives, so that part looks settled.

content.text: Two useful details came out of this. The measure would apply to pending lawsuits and proceedings already underway, and the labor rules tie into Section 21183.5. I'll confirm exactly what 21183.5 requires, since the labor provisions matter to some voters.

assistantMessageEvent.content:
I'm going through what 21183.5 requires for the non-housing essential projects Prop 45 covers. Private projects need prevailing wages and a trained workforce with reporting and penalties, with PLA exceptions, while public agency projects need a trained workforce through commitments or PLAs. So Prop 45's labor terms look substantive and pro-labor for those projects.

I'm weighing whether the workforce rules for housing are weaker than SB 35's, since the prevailing wage rule for housing seems to apply only to buildings over 85 feet. I'm checking how 21015 limits that prevailing wage provision to tall essential housing.

So for housing under 85 feet, this chapter seems to impose no prevailing wage requirement, and the 21183.5 labor standards are explicitly excluded for essential housing. Only buildings over 85 feet pick up the prevailing wage rule, along with the contractor liability provision.

Housing under 85 feet appears to get no prevailing-wage requirement under this measure, since the labor standards in 21183.5 are excluded for essential housing and the prevailing-wage rule only reaches buildings over 85 feet. That makes the labor terms noticeably weaker for housing than for the non-housing projects.

I'm double-checking that housing under 85 feet gets no prevailing-wage requirement, since the essential housing definition doesn't carry the 21183.5 labor terms. Other essential categories do, so the exclusion holds. I'm also noting that the Global ELR piece says the measure would reach agency proceedings and lawsuits already underway, which is a retroactivity point worth keeping.

I'm checking whether the measure has any sunset clause, whether the Legislature or Governor has signaled a response, and whether a competing measure could undo it, since those are the last gaps I want to close.

I'm checking whether any other measure on the ballot could conflict with Prop 45 or whether Prop 37 or Prop 1 touches essential project review, and I don't think either does, so I'm setting that aside. I'm also looking at the wildfire-risk definitions and the forest thinning concerns, which I've already covered.

I'm checking the cost claim next: the roughly $75,000 per-home savings figure traces to supporters' estimates, not to anything the measure itself establishes, so I'll note it as a claim rather than a finding.

I'm checking the LAO's estimate of potential annual costs, then looking at the "No" side's claims about the Legislative Counsel letter, which I'll treat as contested rather than settled. I'm also considering whether any provision might face a constitutional challenge, such as the legal defense clause or limits on court remedies.

I'm now checking whether the measure's "occupies the field" language in 21030 would preempt local rules on essential projects, such as local moratoriums or CEQA thresholds, which would bear directly on local control. The LAO and most coverage don't dwell on this, though the local-control angle is worth noting.

I'm checking the measure's "occupies the field" language in section 21030, which would seem to preempt local rules on how essential projects are reviewed and approved. That could limit cities' ability to impose stricter standards or moratoriums, even though the campaign materials say local authority is preserved.

Next I'm checking whether local agencies still have power to approve or deny essential projects under 21014(a) and 21025(g), or whether the measure's rules on how they review those projects leave them much less room. I'm also weighing the "occupies the field" language against the claim that cities keep their authority, since that is where the local-control conflict would come from.

I'm now summarizing what Prop 45 covers: its "essential" categories include market-rate housing, water, clean energy, medical facilities, first responder and wildfire-risk work, broadband, education, and transportation, with related infrastructure included. The exclusions are narrow, such as jails, new oil and gas production, high-speed rail, Delta conveyance, nuclear, and detention facilities.

I'm now going through the procedural side of the opt-in path: a 30-day completeness check, a 365-business-day deadline for EIRs and 180 days for shorter reviews, and public comment windows of 45 and 20 days. Once a deadline passes, the applicant can force a hearing and sue, and the measure also freezes the rules in effect when the application was filed.

I'm noting the remaining procedural rules: a 30-day window to file suit, a 270-day court deadline that can be extended by 90 days, and review limited to objective legal requirements under a substantial-evidence standard. I'm also checking the labor terms, where non-housing essential projects must meet the 21183.5 standards, housing under 85 feet is exempt, and taller housing must pay prevailing wages.

Next I'm pulling together the political backing: CalChamber sponsors the measure alongside CBIA and the Brin/Doerr-backed Building a Better California, with utilities, Prologis, and housing developers among the supporters, while the No side claims data center developers spent roughly $1M in the final week.

Now I'm noting who backs the measure and who opposes it, from the lists of endorsers and campaign groups, including the local papers and outlets that have weighed in.

I'm now going through the rest of the opposition and neutral lineup: environmental, public health, and nurse groups, along with Tom Steyer and Rep. Jared Huffman, plus several county GOP parties on the other side. On the editorial and political front, Newsom has reportedly not taken a position but criticized "problematic provisions," Wiener and California YIMBY are neutral, SPUR offers no recommendation, and the SF Chronicle and Press Democrat editorial boards are against.

I'm now checking the money side: supporters appear to have raised somewhere around $40 to $56 million depending on the report, against roughly $30 million for opponents, so I'll keep those figures as approximate.

I'm weighing whether the status quo is really as broken as the measure assumes, since CEQA has already been amended several times in recent years and reformers like Wiener and the YIMBY groups seem to prefer fixing it through legislation rather than an initiative. The question I keep returning to is whether Prop 45's approach to delays is the efficient fix or an overbroad one.

I'm weighing the measure's cost and reversibility now: the LAO puts initial costs in the tens of millions per year, possibly over $100M, with long-term savings uncertain. Amending it would need a two-thirds legislative vote and has to stay consistent with its purposes, so if voters later find problems, fixing them won't be easy.

I'm weighing the lock-in risk: amending the measure takes a two-thirds legislative vote and must stay consistent with its purposes, so a "No" vote would leave room for narrower, adjustable reforms. I'm also noting how broad "essential" is, covering most housing, ancillary infrastructure, transmission, broadband, and water, and listing the open questions around data centers, the "fullest possible weight" and "objective" standards, field preemption, retroactivity, and tribal consultation.

I'm weighing the case for the measure: its environmental and legal protections mostly stay in place, the housing and infrastructure delay problem is real and costly, and some CEQA experts see parts of it as sensible reform. Public support was strong in July and September but has slipped, with the latest polling narrowly against, so the affordability framing may still sway some voters.

I'm leaning toward "No" as my answer, since the measure's broad scope and the two-thirds lock-in make it hard to fix later if it goes wrong. I'll be upfront that this is a close call that depends on whether faster housing and infrastructure matter more to you than the process trade-offs, and I'll say what would change my answer.

I'm checking whether "Yes" could be the stronger choice for someone who weighs housing and infrastructure delays most heavily, such as a housing advocate or a resident of a city where CEQA lawsuits have stalled a transit or clean energy project. The LAO's possible long-term savings, the Mercury News's "fairer, less expensive and more predictable" framing, and the YIMBY-aligned support all make that a reasonable position rather than a fringe one.

I'm settling on "No" as the more defensible recommendation: the measure is sweeping and hard to amend, its benefits aren't guaranteed (there's no affordability requirement), and its scope is broad and ambiguous, covering data centers, sprawl, and ancillary infrastructure. The Legislature is also already pursuing targeted CEQA reforms, so a "No" vote doesn't leave the problem unaddressed.

I'm checking the Legislature's recent record, noting AB 130, SB 131, SB 79, and SB 887 as targeted changes already in motion, which makes a "No" vote less likely to leave the problem unaddressed. assistantMessageEvent.content:
**No.**

It's a values call, but here's my basis, using the full measure text and coverage through Nov. 2, 2026:

- **The court limits are the real change, not the deadlines.** Challengers could only argue violations of "objective" existing laws. Courts could halt only the noncompliant part of a project, not rescind an approval. The rules would also apply to lawsuits already pending.
- **Public input shrinks under the new process, even for projects nobody sues.** Only about 2% of CEQA projects get sued each year, per the Little Hoover Commission. But comment periods are capped at 20 or 45 days, most late comments are excluded from the record, and applicants who use the fast track can limit the analysis to one alternative of their own design.
- **Benefits aren't guaranteed, and the scope is broad.** "Essential" covers market-rate housing and related infrastructure, and nothing requires affordability or lower prices. The "$75,000 per home" savings figure comes from supporters. Whether data centers qualify is disputed.
- **It's hard to undo.** Amendments require a two-thirds legislative vote and must further the measure's purposes. Support has also dropped from 73% in July to 46% in PPIC's final poll (50% no).

**The case for yes:** CEQA delays are real. The measure doesn't exempt projects from environmental review, local agencies keep approval power, and most non-housing projects would face labor standards, including prevailing wages for private developers. If faster housing, water, clean energy, and wildfire projects matter more to you than weaker review and court access, yes is a defensible vote.

Some provisions are ambiguous, such as whether the court limits apply to every eligible project or only to applicants who opt in. Courts would have to settle that after passage.

content.text:
**No.**

It's a values call, but here's my basis, using the full measure text and coverage through Nov. 2, 2026:

- **The court limits are the real change, not the deadlines.** Challengers could only argue violations of "objective" existing laws. Courts could halt only the noncompliant part of a project, not rescind an approval. The rules would also apply to lawsuits already pending.
- **Public input shrinks under the new process, even for projects nobody sues.** Only about 2% of CEQA projects get sued each year, per the Little Hoover Commission. But comment periods are capped at 20 or 45 days, most late comments are excluded from the record, and applicants who use the fast track can limit the analysis to one alternative of their own design.
- **Benefits aren't guaranteed, and the scope is broad.** "Essential" covers market-rate housing and related infrastructure, and nothing requires affordability or lower prices. The "$75,000 per home" savings figure comes from supporters. Whether data centers qualify is disputed.
- **It's hard to undo.** Amendments require a two-thirds legislative vote and must further the measure's purposes. Support has also dropped from 73% in July to 46% in PPIC's final poll (50% no).

**The case for yes:** CEQA delays are real. The measure doesn't exempt projects from environmental review, local agencies keep approval power, and most non-housing projects would face labor standards, including prevailing wages for private developers. If faster housing, water, clean energy, and wildfire projects matter more to you than weaker review and court access, yes is a defensible vote.

Some provisions are ambiguous, such as whether the court limits apply to every eligible project or only to applicants who opt in. Courts would have to settle that after passage.

content.text:
**No.**

It's a values call, but here's my basis, using the full measure text and coverage through Nov. 2, 2026:

- **The court limits are the real change, not the deadlines.** Challengers could only argue violations of "objective" existing laws. Courts could halt only the noncompliant part of a project, not rescind an approval. The rules would also apply to lawsuits already pending.
- **Public input shrinks under the new process, even for projects nobody sues.** Only about 2% of CEQA projects get sued each year, per the Little Hoover Commission. But comment periods are capped at 20 or 45 days, most late comments are excluded from the record, and applicants who use the fast track can limit the analysis to one alternative of their own design.
- **Benefits aren't guaranteed, and the scope is broad.** "Essential" covers market-rate housing and related infrastructure, and nothing requires affordability or lower prices. The "$75,000 per home" savings figure comes from supporters. Whether data centers qualify is disputed.
- **It's hard to undo.** Amendments require a two-thirds legislative vote and must further the measure's purposes. Support has also dropped from 73% in July to 46% in PPIC's final poll (50% no).

**The case for yes:** CEQA delays are real. The measure doesn't exempt projects from environmental review, local agencies keep approval power, and most non-housing projects would face labor standards, including prevailing wages for private developers. If faster housing, water, clean energy, and wildfire projects matter more to you than weaker review and court access, yes is a defensible vote.

Some provisions are ambiguous, such as whether the court limits apply to every eligible project or only to applicants who opt in. Courts would have to settle that after passage.

45
MODIFIES ENVIRONMENTAL REVIEW FOR CERTAIN PROJECTS. INITIATIVE STATUTE.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Amends California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) to expedite environmental review for certain projects (including most housing, transportation, water, and health projects) by setting deadlines to complete environmental review and resolve lawsuits challenging project approvals. Fiscal Impact: Initial costs for state and local governments, likely in the high tens of millions of dollars—potentially exceeding $100 million—annually, partly covered by fees. Uncertain, potentially more significant positive or negative longer-term fiscal effects. Supporters: California Children’s Hospital Association; California Water Association; California Council for Affordable Housing Opponents: Coalition for Clean Air; CA Environmental Voters; Physicians for Social Responsibility, LA; National Wildlife Federation
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: Certain public and private projects would be eligible for new project review and court challenge procedures. For example, new procedures would tighten time limits for environmental review and reduce the scope of what courts can consider when reviewing legal challenges.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: Public and private projects would continue to use existing project review and court challenge procedures.

PRO
The failing status quo is making California unaffordable. Prop. 45 fixes our broken system and lowers our high cost of living by cutting red tape to build housing, water, schools, hospitals, clean energy, and wildfire prevention faster—while maintaining California’s strong environmental protections. Vote YES for a more affordable California. YESonProp45.com

PROPOSITION 45 LIMITS ENVIRONMENTAL AND PUBLIC REVIEW OF PROJECTS BUILT IN YOUR COMMUNITY. Prop. 45 won’t lower your costs: its utility and corporate funders profit while taxpayers pay more. VOTE NO.

OFFICIAL TITLE AND SUMMARY
PREPARED BY THE ATTORNEY GENERAL
Amends California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) to expedite environmental review for specified project categories (including most housing, transportation, water, health, wildfire mitigation, educational facility, internet access, and clean energy projects). For these types of projects, this measure:
Sets deadlines for public agencies to complete environmental review and take required actions.
Allows expedited review of environmental impacts, limiting public agencies’ current obligation to consider a range of feasible project alternatives to reduce environmental impacts.
Establishes deadlines for filing and resolving lawsuits challenging project approvals; limits evidence courts may consider and relief courts can order.
SUMMARY OF LEGISLATIVE ANALYST'S ESTIMATE OF NET STATE AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT FISCAL IMPACT:
Initial costs for state and local governments, likely in the high tens of millions of dollars annually—potentially exceeding $100 million annually—to implement new project review and court challenge procedures for eligible projects. Fees paid by project applicants and people filing lawsuits would partly cover these costs.
In the longer term, uncertain, but potentially more significant positive or negative fiscal effects for state and local governments. The overall effect depends, in part, on how the new procedures change the number of eligible projects that get built and whether those projects have different environmental impacts.
